subject: Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable

messages.author: 394893f1497d29a3
messages.subject: Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable
parts:
Hello everyone,

 

I’m new to rStan and Bayesian statistics, so I currently have limited knowledge of both, but require it for my research. I’m running a mixed-effects model on a dataset of 4000 observations (200 groups each with 20 cases). The model is quite extensive, 99 population-level effects (both binary and continuous) and 13 random-effects. Running this model on the cluster succeeds in 4 to 5 hours and gives me interpretable output.

 

In the analysis of this output I noticed the presence of heteroscedasticity looking at the plot of fitted values versus residual values. Experimentation on a smaller model (using the lme4 package) showed that taking the inverse of the response variable (1/Y) seems to solve this issue. I want to run the larger regression model using rStan and the inverse transformation of Y, but this requires an enormous amount of time to run. Running the model with 4000 iterations (1000 warmup) requires more than 8 days to finish and returns 2900 divergent transitions and many Rhats above 1.1. I do not want to run it with more iterations as it already takes so long to run.

Maybe it has something to do with the response values after the inverse transformation, which are very close to zero.

Y:            min=7183.004,                 max=88021.06,                 mean=35940.4

1/Y          min=1.136092e-5             max=0.0001392175           mean=3.741544e-05

 

i have been looking for a solution to the issue a long time, so if anybody has a helpful suggestion it would be most welcome. Thanks in advance.


Jeroen


(p.s. Before I found out about this mailing list, I posted a less detailed version of this question on Stackoverflow where I was suggested to use the 'QR=TRUE' argument to stan_lmer, but this did not resolve the issue unfortunately.)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable
parts:
I'd recommend not waiting four days for answers. You usually won't
need 4000 iterations with Stan for well-behaved programs.

You might want to try RStanArm if you already have a working lme4
version.

In general, you want to rescale your variables so that the
parameters are roughly unit scale (0 mean, 1 std dev) in the posterior
wherever possible (on the unconstrained scale). You
can deconvolve everything back to the original scales afterward.
That goes for both the Y and 1/Y cases. Very small or large values cause
the adaptation to struggle in the same way that ill-conditioned matrices
(high ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue) cause algebraic problems
in factoring them.

You'll also have problems if you have predictors that are highly
correlated.

Also, with this:

vector[N] Z_1_1;
vector[N] Z_1_2;
vector[N] Z_1_3;
vector[N] Z_1_4;
vector[N] Z_1_5;
vector[N] Z_1_6;
vector[N] Z_1_7;
vector[N] Z_1_8;
vector[N] Z_1_9;
vector[N] Z_1_10;
vector[N] Z_1_11;
vector[N] Z_1_12;
vector[N] Z_1_13;

you can just define

vector[N] Z_1[13];

and same for the r variables and then you can just do usual vector/matrix
operations on them.

You might also try adding tighter priors and including priors for all
the parameters (such as b).

- Bob

messages.author: 394893f1497d29a3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable
parts:
Thanks for the suggestions. I tried rescaling by standardizing the numerical predictor variables (dividing by their standard deviation as they were already centred) and this made the sampling go a lot faster. It took almost 27 hours to run 4 chains in parallel with 1000 warm-up iterations and 3000 post-warmup iterations. However, the model did not converge, all group-level effects had Rhats larger than 1.1. Specifying tighter priors gave convergency problems as well (also when specifying a prior for all population-level effects).

I did discover an alternative that runs faster and converges perfectly. Simply multiplying the 1/Y values with a large constant (1 000 000 in my case) did the trick. This time, it took nearly 12 hours to complete and gave no convergency problems.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable
parts:
Thanks for reporting back. We really need to improve our
adaptation because we should be able to learn these marginal
scales during warmup.

We generally recommend 50% of the iterations be devoted to
warmup. At most that'll cost 50% efficiency, but it has
a higher chance of adaptation converging, especially in
ill conditioned problems.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling very slow after inverse transformation of response variable
parts:
The fix was rescaling the parameters by 10^{6}, which
implied that the original model had a condition number
of at least 10^{6} which is going to be hard for _any_
adaptive algorithm.
